metadata.title: Students’ growth mindset: Relation to teacher beliefs, teaching practices, and school climate

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses OECD Survey on Social and Emotional Skills (SSES) data from the city of Helsinki, Finland, with a two-stage stratified sampling design (schools selected with probability proportional to size, then students randomly selected within sampled schools). The analytic sample was restricted to students with matching teacher and principal data (N=2200). The manuscript does not report the use of complex survey weights (e.g., student/sampling weights) or any replicate-weight scheme, and it instead estimates multilevel Bayesian probit models in Mplus. Because the analysis is not framed as an ML prediction pipeline and no weight variable names are provided, weighting strategy details are not available from the text.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable is a single-item Likert-scale measure of students’ intelligence growth mindset (reverse coded), not a cognitive achievement score with plausible values. Therefore, plausible values handling is not applicable because PVs are not generated for this type of non-cognitive attitude outcome in the SSES instrument. For missing data, the authors state that missingness on the mindset item was minimal and that they retained all cases, but they do not describe a formal missing-data method (e.g., listwise deletion, imputation, or model-based handling) in a way that maps to the schema categories.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used the Finnish SSES sample from the city of Helsinki and focused on 10-year-old students. From 3071 surveyed 10-year-olds, the analytic sample was restricted to students with matching teacher and principal data (N=2200). Missing mindset responses were retained because missingness was minimal and no systematic class-level missing-data patterns were identified; robustness checks indicated that omitting students with missing growth mindset did not change results.

main_findings.dataset_used: OECD SSES 2018-2020 (Finland, Helsinki) Grade/age: 10-year-olds (elementary) — student mindset (single-item Likert)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel Bayesian probit path analysis (random intercept model): guided inquiry β=0.41, 95% CI [0.11, 0.68], p<.01; task differentiation β=-0.56, 95% CI [-0.79, -0.22], p<.01; holistic development β=0.43, 95% CI [0.01, 0.73], p=.04. Variance partition: classroom 4.7% and school 5.5% of variance; teacher-level factors explained R2=0.56 of between-class variation; school-level factors accounted for 12% of between-school variation.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using OECD SSES 2018–2020 (Finland, Helsinki) data for 10-year-old elementary students, the study leveraged guided inquiry, task differentiation, and schools’ holistic development emphasis (plus related teaching/practice variables) to model students’ intelligence growth mindset, finding that guided inquiry and holistic development were positively associated with growth mindset while task differentiation was negatively associated. This indicates that teacher instructional approaches that support learning through guided inquiry and avoid ability-based task assignment may help cultivate early growth-mindset beliefs, though the correlational design limits causal claims.

data.outcome_summary: This study used OECD Survey on Social and Emotional Skills (SSES) data collected in 2018–2020 from the city of Helsinki, Finland, focusing on 10-year-old students and linking student, teacher, and principal reports (final sample: 2200 students, 358 teachers, 65 principals). The authors estimated multilevel Bayesian probit models to predict students’ intelligence growth mindset measured by a single reverse-coded 5-point Likert item, accounting for the nested structure (students within classrooms within schools). In the random-intercept model, guided inquiry showed a positive association with growth mindset (β=0.41, 95% CI [0.11, 0.68], p<.01), task differentiation showed a negative association (β=-0.56, 95% CI [-0.79, -0.22], p<.01), and schools’ holistic development emphasis was positively associated (β=0.43, 95% CI [0.01, 0.73], p=.04). Classroom and school contexts explained about 4.7% and 5.5% of variance, respectively. Limitations include cross-sectional correlational inference and the use of a single-item outcome, with missing-data handling described qualitatively rather than via a formal imputation/deletion method.
